title: Stop Doing foot tendon training Wrong: Train Your foot tendons Instead
description: Every step you take is powered by cables inside your feet that most training never touches. The toe raise number exposes them in sixty seconds, and it predicts more about your speed and balance than any calf photo. Get your number, meet the foot cables, and start wiring them today.

scenes.narration: Stand tall, barefoot, with your heels planted and your feet flat. Now lift all ten toes off the floor as high as they go, squeeze for one second, and lower them slowly. That is one rep. For the next sixty seconds, count how many clean reps you can do without your heels rocking, your knees bending, or your toes barely leaving the ground. The last few reps should burn deep inside the arch and up the front of your shin. Stop the clock at sixty and write the number down. It feels like a party trick. It is actually a direct readout of the tendon system that launches every step, cut, and jump you will ever make. Keep your number. At the end of this video I will tell you exactly what it says about your feet.

beats.title: NOT A PARTY TRICK
lines: that launch every step you take.

scenes.label: THE LINE BETWEEN FLAT AND WIRED
scenes.sub: under 15: sleepy feet - over 45: sprinter's feet
scenes.narration: Here is the line. Thirty clean toe raises in a minute is where a normal foot becomes a wired one. Under fifteen, your foot tendons are simply asleep, and asleep is fixable. Between fifteen and thirty, the cables are waking up but they fade early, which is why your feet tire on long walks. Over forty five, you own feet that most runners would trade for, because this system almost never gets trained on purpose. Whatever your number is, it is not a life sentence. It is a starting measurement, and this is one of the fastest numbers on the whole channel to move.

Look at the shape of a foot. Twenty six bones, and almost none of them move because of muscles inside the foot itself. The real engines sit up in your calf and shin, and they reach into the foot through long tendons that run under the arch like cables under a bridge. The biggest of them pulls on your big toe, and it is the last thing that touches the ground on every step. When you lift your toes, you are tensioning that whole cable network at once. When you lower slowly, you are teaching it to be strong while it lengthens, which is exactly the job it does when you run. Your arch is not a passive shape. It is a bow, and the tendons are its string.

Here is what happens when that bow works. Every time your foot lands, the arch flattens slightly and the tendons stretch, storing energy like a spring being pulled. Every time you push off, they snap that energy back into the ground for free. Studies of running estimate that the arch and its tendons return a meaningful share of each stride's energy, which is why tired feet make your whole body feel slow. Shoes with thick foam do part of this job for you, and like any helper, they let the worker get weak. Your toe raise number is low because your springs have had a assistant for years. The good news is that springs respond to training exactly like muscles do, just on a slower clock.

beats.text: PUSH OFF: IT PAYS YOU BACK

scenes.narration: Most people train their feet the wrong way, if they train them at all. They buy softer shoes, add thicker insoles, and wrap the problem in more padding. That is training the foot to do less. The tendon system adapts to the opposite signal: honest load, applied slowly, repeated often. That is why the toe raise works. It is small, it is boring, and it loads the exact cables that modern life unloaded. There is no machine in the gym for this, no shortcut product, and no hack. There is just a floor, your bodyweight, and sixty seconds. The guys who fix their feet do it with daily minutes, not with shopping.

Before we train it, audit it. Your foot tendons work a longer shift than any other tissue you own. A normal day hands them five to ten thousand steps, and every single one is a small stretch and release of the arch cables. This is why the toe raise number predicts things that seem unrelated: why your feet ache on long city days, why your balance fades when you are tired, why the last kilometer of a hike feels twice as long as the first. The cables do not get a vote on the schedule. They work every step or the step does not happen. People blame their shoes, their age, their job. The honest variable is almost always capacity: the cables were given a ten thousand step job and a two thousand step training history. Close that gap, and the whole day gets cheaper. That is what the protocol coming up is really doing, one quiet day of toe raises at a time.

Now the part nobody tells skinny guys. Your feet carry less weight than a heavy guy's feet with every single step, and that sounds like a disadvantage. Flip it. It means you can train your foot tendons every day without beating them up, stack hundreds of quality reps a week, and recover overnight. The heavy guy's feet are already near their limit just walking around. Yours have spare capacity, and spare capacity is where fast adaptation lives. Your light frame is not the reason your feet are weak. It is the reason they can get strong faster than almost anyone's, once you actually point training at them.
Train with me. Four rounds of toe raises, forty seconds of work, twenty seconds of rest. Heels planted, toes high, lower them slowly, and chase the burn in the arch. Go.

Here is your week. Toe raises once a day, two minutes total, ideally barefoot on a hard floor. Add towel scrunches twice a week: lay a towel flat, and drag it toward you with your toes, one foot at a time. Walk barefoot at home whenever you can, and let the floor do its old job. Progress is simple: when sixty seconds feels easy, slow every rep down to three seconds up and three seconds down. One warning that matters. Sharp foot pain is not training, and if pain in the arch or heel sticks around for more than a couple of weeks, see a professional and get it checked. Tendons reward patience and punish stubbornness.

scenes.label: THE RETEST LINE IN 30 DAYS
scenes.sub: under 15: untrained - 15 to 30: building - over 30: wired
scenes.narration: So, your number. Under fifteen: your foot cables are untrained, not broken, and daily work will move this faster than almost any other test on the channel. Fifteen to thirty: you are building, and the slow reps are your next level. Over thirty: your feet are wired, and you are ready to load them harder. Put your number in the comments. Just the number. We retest in thirty days, and I want to see that first number again next to your new one.

Your feet are the foundation every other number on this channel stands on. Wire them, and the jumps, the sprints, and the balance all get a free upgrade. Retest in thirty days and bring me a bigger number. Subscribe so you do not miss the retest. This is {channel}. Train the cable.
